strategy.summary: Dichtungswerk Ravensteiner is a sound, group-owned seal maker (parent Ravensteiner Holding AG). It is capacity-full and allocating standard mechanical seals. We are a small customer to it. It wants binding, long commitments, not cash. Our position differs by part. On 340010 it is our single source and owns the tooling, so we are weak; its price is well above our own-plant should-cost, so margin is healthy. On 340011 it is the minority dual source behind a cheaper Kohlering, so we are strong. On 340030 we have a cheaper qualified alternative (Elasto-Dicht), but that quote is old, and Ravensteiner's delivery on this part is poor. History: it asks modestly and settles far lower, often at zero. Increases above its threshold need its pricing committee, which meets fortnightly. Prices are fixed per calendar year with a notice period, so watch whether notice for next year arrives in time. Strategy: trade binding volume and contract length for price stability and secured allocation on 340010. Use rival prices on 340011 and 340030. Keep the tone respectful; threats would backfire with a supplier that can deprioritise us.
strategy.decision_maker: Key account manager for moves within the pricing threshold; above it, the supplier's pricing committee, which meets every two weeks. Day-to-day contact is a new inside-sales colleague (doc:20251108-70410-N, doc:20260310-70410-M1).

price_view.reasoning: 340010 has a large margin over should-cost, but scarcity and single sourcing limit pressure: aim to hold price in exchange for commitment. 340011 has room down toward the rival's price. 340030 has room per the rival quote, but the rubber index supports a small increase and the quote is old. findings.text: part:340010 (24 mm seal, single source): price EUR 29.89 sits +23.0% above our bottom-up should-cost of EUR 24.31 for this supplier's own plant (no margin, ±5%). That gap is a healthy margin and the clearest room on price among its parts.

part:340011 (32 mm seal): price EUR 38.29 is +10.2% above a should-cost of EUR 34.74. That estimate models the plant of sup:70440, not Ravensteiner, so it is weaker evidence. Kohlering (sup:70440) sells the same part to us at EUR 37.55, 1.9% below Ravensteiner. Ravensteiner also lost the 2024 benchmark at 41.55 vs 40.23.

part:340030 (aramid gasket): we have no should-cost. In the 2025 benchmark, Elasto-Dicht quoted EUR 1.97 against our current EUR 2.23 (-11.7%), with an 8-day lead time vs 49. Ravensteiner was awarded at 2.35 yet bills 2.23. This quote is the main price lever on this part, but it is 16 months old.

Cost drivers justify only small increases. Labour (LCI-C) rose +2.7% and rubber (PPI-C2219) +3.9% over 12 months, both at their 36-month peak. Weighted, that implies about +1.3% on 340010, +1.5% on 340011 and +2.5% on 340030. Prices have been flat since 2024/2025, so the supplier can claim a cumulative catch-up of roughly 3-6% since its last change. That claim is still well inside the 340010 margin.
Market news it may cite is irrelevant to seals: copper +48%, electronic boards +41% and steel +7.3% are not in its cost drivers. Power is -43% vs 2022, which argues against energy-based claims.

The supplier usually settles well below its ask: a 1.7-2.7 pp gap, with +0% settled last round on all three parts. Its pricing committee approves increases above 2%. Capacity is tight (allocation, binding-commitment demand), which strengthens its hand on 340010, where it is our single source.

findings.text: Decision structure: price changes above 2% need approval from a pricing committee that meets every two weeks. The key account manager cannot move beyond 2% alone. Expect pauses of about 2 weeks between substantive moves. Offers that stay at or below 2% can likely be settled at KAM level.

The supplier is capacity-constrained and acting from strength. It reported very strong order intake in March. In August it announced it is allocating standard mechanical seals in line with last year's call-offs. On 2026-09-18 it refused our full forecast for part:340010, said lead times are longer than agreed, and will prioritise customers with firm long-term commitments.

What it wants is binding commitment, not cash. It explicitly asks for a binding 12-month commitment, and long-term firm volume is its stated priority currency. Allocation is based on last year's call-offs (19,360 units for 340010). Our forecast of 21,310 units exceeds that, so the extra volume is exactly what is at risk.

It is financially sound and not dependent on us. It is group-owned (Ravensteiner Holding AG) with 650 staff and EUR 151M turnover. Equity ratio is 28.8% and the credit index is stable at 159. Our spend is about 0.5% of its turnover, so we are a small customer and it can afford to deprioritise us.

Our payment record is a mild sensitivity. We pay reliably on average, but 76.4% of invoices are late, by about 2 days on average and a maximum of 6. Payment terms are 30 days net, already shorter than our 60-day standard. Faster or more punctual payment could be a cheap give.

The contact changed: inside sales has been our sales contact since October 2025. The relationship may be less senior than before, and escalation to the KAM or committee may be needed for real decisions.

Weaknesses in its position:
- Delivery is poor at 79.5% on time against a 95% target, which conflicts with any capacity premium.
- Historically it settles well below its asks, at +0.0% in the last round.
- Prices are fixed per calendar year, and changes need 90 days' notice before year end.

findings.text: The framework agreement ctr:4600070410 runs 2025-07-01 to 2027-06-30. It covers all three parts. Prices are fixed per calendar year. Any change for 2027 needs written notice at least 90 days before year end, so by about 2026-10-02. An increase notified later cannot apply before 2028 unless we agree to it.
The contract extends by 12 months unless terminated with 90 days' notice. Our exit notice must reach them by 2027-04-01. That is a credible lever, but realistic only for 340011 and 340030.

Payment is 30 days net, against our standard of 60, so they already have a payment benefit. Delivery is DAP with a 42-day lead time. The quality agreement sets a 95% on-time target and a EUR 150 flat fee per supplier-caused complaint.

Their history across 9 renewals is to ask about 1-7% and settle far lower. Settlements were 0% in 6 of 9 cases. The largest settlement was 3.7%, on 340030 in 2024. For the 2026 renewals they asked 1.1-2.5% and settled 0% on all three parts. Their key account manager said changes above 2% need their pricing committee.

Dependency by part:
- part:340010: they are our single source at 100% quota and own the tooling. This is our weakest position, and they currently refuse to confirm our full forecast.
- part:340011: dual-sourced, with Kohlering-Technik (sup:70440) holding 60% at a lower price. The 2024 RFQ was awarded to sup:70440. Strong for us.
- part:340030: they hold 100%, but sup:70430 is qualified and quoted 11.7% lower in rfq:6000000118. Strong for us.

We are a small customer to them: about EUR 816k, roughly 0.5% of their EUR 151M turnover. They are financially sound and group owned. They are allocating standard mechanical seals and want firm 12-month commitments, so their leverage is real on the mechanical seals.

findings.text: Delivery is the weak spot and is not improving: on time to the requested date has been stuck around 78-82% for three years. It stands at 79.5% for the 12 months to 2026-09 (78.7% a year earlier), against a contractual target of 95% and a peer median of 84.6%. Even against its own confirmed dates it reaches only 85.9%. When late, it is late by 18.2 days on average, up to 36 days. The scorecard still shows class A green, which blunts our case: the supplier will point to it.

The delivery problem sits mainly on casing gasket part:340030: 70.4% on time to the requested date, 25.9% late, up to 36 days late. Parts 340010 and 340011 are at about 84%. Its first confirmations also slip, e.g. po:4500014369-10 was confirmed 2 days after the requested date. For 340010, average lateness when late is 20 days, which matters because it is our single source.

Quality argues its case. Rolling ppm fell from 476 (2025Q3) to 270 (2026Q3), against a peer median of 457, with 0 overdue 8Ds. Complaints are frequent but small (mostly 1 piece each), and the EUR 150 flat recharges total only about EUR 4,950 over three years. Defects are therefore a minor cost driver; using them as a price lever is weak. One open 8D remains: qn:20005012 on part 340011 (porosity) has no D8 date yet.

Recurring defect types on 340030 and 340010 show the 8Ds are not stopping repeats. The same defects keep returning: coating defects, burrs, wrong material certificates and missing markings. This supports a ppm commitment or chargeback term rather than a price cut.

Our volume outlook is up about 10% on every part. It was shared with the supplier, so it carries weight. 340010: 21,310 forecast vs 19,360 ordered. 340011: 12,720 vs 11,420 in total, of which about 40% falls to this supplier. 340030: 30,600 vs 27,780. Ordered volumes were flat through 2024-2026, and earlier forecasts overshot actuals by 10-18%, so the supplier may discount our forecast. However, it is allocating capacity and wants binding 12-month commitments. A volume commitment is therefore our main currency, not a giveaway.

Prices have been flat at the 2025/2026 level and rose only 2-4% since 2023. Should-cost on 340010 is 23% below its price, and for 340030 a qualified alternative quoted 11.7% lower. Supply is tight, though: the supplier is allocating volumes and cannot confirm the full forecast for 340010.

arguments.text: Capacity is fully booked and standard mechanical seals are on allocation based on last year's call-offs. We can only secure your full 340010 forecast (21,310 pcs for the next 12 months) for customers who give firm, long-term commitments. Price stability and a guaranteed allocation together are worth something.

Our prices have been flat since the last renewals: 340010 since 2024, 340011 and 340030 since 2025. Over the same period German manufacturing labour costs rose 2.7 % and rubber product prices rose 3.9 %, and both indices are at their 36-month peak. On 340030 rubber is the main driver. A modest catch-up is fair; we are not asking for a windfall.
We have a track record of moderation. We settled at zero in the 2025 and 2026 rounds on all three parts, absorbing cost increases for Hollerau. That goodwill is now spent.

The quality trend is clearly improving: ppm fell from 476 to 270 and complaints from 23 to 14. We have no overdue 8D reports and remain class A green on your own scorecard. We are also financially sound, with an equity ratio of 28.8 % and a stable credit index, so we are a safe supply base.
On 340030 the Elasto-Dicht quote of 1.97 is more than a year old with only 14 days' validity. In that same RFQ we were awarded at 2.35, and today you still pay 2.23.
Price changes above 2 % need our pricing committee, which meets every two weeks. I can move quickly within that band.

weak_points: 340010 at 29.89 sits about 23 % above Hollerau's should-cost estimate of 24.31. However, that estimate's confidence is only 5 %, so I would dispute it.
Delivery performance is poor: 79.5 % on time against the requested date versus a 95 % target, with 340030 at only 70.4 % and up to 36 days late. Our own 42-day lead time is now being exceeded.
On 340011 Kohlering is cheaper at 37.55 versus our 38.29, holds 60 % of the volume, and beat us in the 2024 RFQ (40.23 vs 41.55). Hollerau could shift share away from us.
On 340030 a qualified alternative exists that is cheaper and much faster (8 days vs our 49).
Copper and electronics price rises are irrelevant to us. Iron castings are only +1.8 %, and power prices are well down on 2022. Our material share on 340010 is small (3.40 of cost).
Any increase for 2027 needs written notice 90 days before year end, i.e. by about 2 October 2026. If we miss that, the 2027 prices stay fixed.
Recurring quality defects persist (coating, burrs, wrong certificates), and qn:20005012 on 340011 is still open without an 8D close-out.
wants: A binding 12-24 month volume commitment on 340010, ideally with a contract extension beyond June 2027.
A modest increase of about 2-3 % on 340030, and price held at least flat on 340010.
An index clause on PPI-C2219 for the rubber-heavy 340030 as an alternative to a fixed increase.
Keeping our 40 % share on 340011, or more if we match Kohlering.
Firm forecasts or call-offs to smooth our allocation planning.
red_lines: No price cut on 340010 while we are on allocation.
No guaranteed full allocation on 340010 without a binding commitment.
No lower price on 340030 than the current 2.23 unless volume is fully committed for 24 months.
No penalties or chargebacks beyond the EUR 150 flat fee.
Nothing above 2 % agreed without committee approval; no instant concessions beyond that.
red_team.opening: Thank the customer for a long relationship and reliable payment, and acknowledge their need for supply security. Explain the capacity situation and allocation calmly. Offer secured allocation of the full 340010 forecast at an unchanged 29.89 against a binding 24-month volume commitment and contract extension. Propose +2.5 % on 340030 citing the rubber index at its peak, with an index clause as an alternative. Keep 340011 flat, with openness to align with the market if our share grows. Make sure formal written notice is sent before the contractual deadline.

rebuttals.answer: We understand that your capacity is full and that allocation follows last year's call-offs, and we are prepared to make the firm commitment you ask for. That gives you exactly the planning security you describe. In return we expect a guaranteed allocation at the current price, not a higher one. A firm commitment is the consideration for stability. It is not a reason to pay more, and your margin on this part comfortably carries the commitment.

The index movements are real, and we do not dispute them. Weighted by their share of each part's cost, however, they support well under one percent on both mechanical seals. Only on the gasket, where rubber dominates, do they support something more noticeable. Energy, the other usual driver, has fallen sharply. Prices have also not been static: each part has risen since our first orders. We can discuss a catch-up on the gasket within what its index supports. On the seals, the cost effect is small enough to be absorbed.

We appreciate the moderation in recent rounds. It was matched on our side: we paid reliably throughout, and we kept growing our volumes with you. Those rounds also followed increases that both parties agreed were adequate at the time. Moderation has been the shared basis of this relationship, and we would like to continue it rather than treat it as a debt to be repaid.

We recognise the improvement in quality and your financial strength, and we value both. Delivery also remains well below the agreed on-time target. Good quality is what the quality agreement already expects at today's price, so it does not justify an increase. We would welcome a ppm commitment that locks in the improved level.

It is fair to say the alternative quote is not recent. It was nevertheless clearly lower and offered a far shorter lead time, and that supplier remains qualified for the part. Your award came after the price was brought down to today's level, not at the quoted figure. On this part your on-time delivery is the weakest of the three. That makes the current price, rather than a higher one, the reasonable reference.

Thank you, that is helpful. We are happy to keep any agreement within the band you can approve yourself, so that neither side waits on committee cycles. Given the modest cost effect, a result inside that band, tied to a firm volume commitment, seems well within reach.
